name: Oxygen
tagline: A hosted AI agent that takes a goal, plans, calls tools, and reports back.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The core of any agent product is a loop: send context to a model, let it pick a tool, run the tool, feed the result back, repeat until done. That loop is genuinely a one-sitting build and a competent agent will write you a working version with file, shell, and HTTP tools before lunch. What you cannot conjure is the boring part around it: a sandbox that stops a confused model from deleting your home directory, retry and cost accounting, a decent UI for watching long runs, and pre-wired connectors to whatever systems you actually want touched. It also stays permanently tethered to somebody else's model API, so this is not a clean independence story, it is a cheaper and more inspectable one. Good trade if you like reading logs, bad trade if you wanted a product.
coreLoopDIY: A local CLI agent that takes a plain-English goal and iterates a model plus tool-call loop over your files, shell, and the web until it declares the task done, logging every step.
requirements: An API key for a frontier model, with a real token budget
Willingness to run shell commands suggested by a model, ideally inside a container
whatYouLose: Sandboxing and blast-radius controls that someone else already stress-tested
Prebuilt connectors to SaaS tools, so every integration is yours to write and maintain
A watchable UI for long runs, plus shareable run history
Model routing and fallback when your one provider rate-limits or degrades
Any notion of safety review on destructive actions beyond your own confirm prompt
moatNotes: Agent loops are commodity. Guardrails, connectors, and not-losing-the-thread on a two-hour run are the actual product.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the demo loop and the reliable loop are separated by weeks of unglamorous work. Timeouts, tool schema drift, context window management, partial failures halfway through a multi-step task, and the moment the model decides rm is a reasonable idea. A hosted agent also gets you a sandbox you did not have to configure and a history you can scroll instead of grep. If the agent is doing anything that touches other people's systems, paying someone to own the failure modes is defensible.
notes: The loop is a toy weekend project; the guardrails are the product.
prompt:
Build a local autonomous agent CLI in an empty folder. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Python 3.11+, uv for deps, Typer for the CLI, Rich for terminal output
- Anthropic Python SDK for the model, key read from .env as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY via python-dotenv
- SQLite via stdlib sqlite3 for run history, file agent.db
- No web server, no frontend

Core behaviour:
- Command: agent run "goal text" [--max-steps 25] [--workdir .]
- Maintain a message list. Each turn, send the goal plus history to the model with tool definitions. Execute the requested tool, append the result, loop until the model returns a final answer or max-steps is hit.
- Tools: read_file(path), write_file(path, content), list_dir(path), run_shell(command), http_get(url)
- All file paths are resolved and confined to --workdir. Reject anything that escapes it.
- run_shell prints the exact command and requires y/N confirmation unless --yolo is passed. Hard 60s timeout, capture stdout and stderr, truncate to 8000 chars.
- Truncate every tool result before it goes back into context, and note when truncation happened.

Observability:
- Persist each run and each step (tool name, args, result preview, token counts if available) to SQLite.
- Commands: agent runs to list past runs, agent show ID to replay one step by step.
- Print running token totals after each step so cost is visible.

Out of scope, do not build: a web UI, multi-agent orchestration, vector memory, provider abstraction layers, Docker sandboxing (just document loudly in the README that shell tools run unsandboxed).

Deliver: pyproject.toml, agent/ package, .env.example, README with install and a worked example. Include pytest tests for path confinement and result truncation using a stubbed model client.
